name: Methylstenbolone (M-Sten / Hybrid)
lead: Methylstenbolone (M-Sten, Methyl-Sten, Ultradrol) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, the 17-alpha-methylated derivative of stenbolone and a delta-1 isomer of methasterone. It was never introduced for medical use and has been sold online as a nutritional supplement or designer steroid.[1][2]

For people trying to build a more muscular, harder-looking physique, it is discussed as an oral way to add size and strength. Users on lifting forums describe it as a strong oral compound that adds hardness and some size, reasoning that androgen receptor activation drives muscle protein accretion in the way other anabolic steroids are said to.[9][10] No clinical trial has measured its effect on muscle, and the published literature concerns detection, metabolism, supplement contents and adverse events.[3][4][5][6]

Because it is sold as a supplement, it has been the subject of toxicology case reports, supplement-analysis papers and anti-doping research. A 2014 case report described cholestatic jaundice in a person using a product containing methylstenbolone and dymethazine, and the compound is prohibited in sport.[6][7]

paras: Methylstenbolone is 2,17alpha-dimethyl-5alpha-androst-1-en-17beta-ol-3-one, a derivative of dihydrotestosterone with a methyl group at carbon 2, a double bond between carbons 1 and 2, and a 17-alpha methyl group.[1] The 17-alpha methylation is associated with oral activity and with a liver burden, a property shared by other 17-alpha-alkylated steroids such as methyltestosterone.[2] Wikipedia lists it as the 17-alpha-methylated form of stenbolone and the delta-1 isomer of methasterone.[1]

It is classified as an androgen receptor agonist.[1] Direct binding and pharmacokinetic data in humans are limited because it never underwent pharmaceutical development; metabolism has been characterised mainly for doping control. Studies in human liver microsomes and a chimeric mouse model, in vivo excretion work and equine studies identified phase I and glucuronide-conjugated urinary metabolites that laboratories use as markers of use.[4][5][7]
A 2022 study of microbial transformation of methylstenbolone produced nine analogues and examined their anti-inflammatory and cytotoxic activity in cell assays.[11]

Wikipedia notes that methylstenbolone was never introduced for medical use.[1] Grokipedia reports a commercial debut around 2011 under the name Ultradrol from a supplement company, sold as a capsule and positioned as a successor to earlier prohormone products; it also reports early detections in seized supplements by 2012. These claims come from a single machine-written source.[2]

A 2013 study identified methylstenbolone in a product sold as a nutritional supplement and described its urinary metabolites, noting that such products are sold online without medical supervision.[3] A 2014 metabolism paper analysed a steroid product labelled as containing it for anti-doping laboratories, which monitor the supplement market.[5] A later review described designer steroids sold as prohormones or testosterone boosters as a growing market, with hepatotoxicity, cholestasis, hypogonadism, gynecomastia and infertility reported among adverse effects of such products.[12]

Methylstenbolone is sold under supplement-style names and is often described in forums as an oral alternative to other 17-alpha-methylated steroids. Several T Nation members say it was legally available in their locality because it was not on a controlled substances list at the time, while others discuss it alongside other orals in terms of side-effect burden.[13][14]

Participants in these forums mention it in stacks with other designer products such as dymethazine-based supplements, recount strength and hardness increases from it, and in several threads describe it as among the more toxic orals on the market, citing the published case reports.[9][10][13][15][16] One poster describes managing appetite loss on orals with liver-support products and many meals.[17] Legal status varies by country and over time; it is prohibited by anti-doping rules.[7]

Published information is limited to case reports, supplement surveillance and extrapolation from related steroids. The 2014 case report described cholestatic jaundice in a user of a product containing methylstenbolone and dymethazine and commented that such products may conceal potent androgens to avoid regulatory scrutiny.[6]

A New York investigation of vitamin supplements found methasterone, dimethazine and methylstenbolone in marketed lots after residents reported fatigue, scalp hair loss and muscle aches and one was hospitalised with liver damage.[8] A review of designer steroids reports hepatotoxicity, cholestasis, renal failure, hypogonadism, gynecomastia and infertility from such products, and describes anabolic steroid use as a possible leading cause of hypogonadism in men of reproductive age.[12] A 2024 analysis of 50 years of case reports links illicit anabolic-androgenic steroid use to reproductive harm.[18]

No studies found of methylstenbolone in a clinical trial. A 2014 case report described cholestatic jaundice in a person using a supplement found to contain methylstenbolone and dymethazine.[6] A 2023 analysis examined androgenic steroids in over-the-counter supplements and adverse health effects.[8] Metabolism and detection studies were done in humans, human liver microsomes, chimeric mice and horses.[3][4][5][7]

lore.intro: On T Nation, methylstenbolone appears in threads on orals, designer supplements and stacks, discussed both as a potent oral and as a compound with a reputation for toxicity.[13][14]

claims.claim: M-Sten adds hardness and some size quickly
claims.believers: Posters say a product containing it was surprisingly strong, hardened their look and added some size by the end of a run.[15]
claims.experts: No clinical trials have measured its effects on muscle or physique; the published literature covers metabolism, detection and adverse events.[3][5]

claims.claim: It is among the more toxic orals
claims.believers: Several members cite the cholestasis case reports and describe it as more toxic than some other orals.[9][16]
claims.experts: A 2014 case report described cholestatic jaundice with a product containing it; 17-alpha alkylation is associated with liver burden, and reviews list hepatotoxicity among adverse effects of designer steroids.[6][12][2]

claims.claim: It is legal where it is not on a controlled substance list
claims.believers: A member notes it was not on the controlled list where they live and was sold in stores.[13]
claims.experts: Regulators and researchers describe such supplement products as unapproved; it is prohibited in sport.[1][7]

claims.claim: Liver support and supplements offset the harm
claims.believers: One user describes running heavy liver support and eating many meals to counter appetite loss.[17]
claims.experts: No published study has tested whether liver-support products protect users of methylstenbolone.

card.summary: An oral designer androgen sold as a supplement or research chemical; no trials, with a case report of cholestatic jaundice.
card.note: Prohibited in sport; liver injury case report.

quick.overview:
Methylstenbolone is an unapproved oral androgen sold online in muscle-building supplements.

Research is mostly about detecting and metabolising it, plus a few case reports.
quick.mechanism: It is classed as an androgen receptor agonist; 17-alpha methylation is associated with oral activity.
quick.risks: A case report links a product containing it to cholestatic jaundice. It is prohibited in sport and has no approved medical use.
